---
title: Browser-hosted sign-in
---

Where the Azure CLI is not an option (Windows, where `az login` keeps its
tokens in the Windows broker, or a machine without `az`), sign in with one
of `dazapiz`'s two interactive credentials instead. Both are the
`azure-identity` classes of the same name, with two additions: their tokens
are cached in the platform's secret store under the name `"dazapiz"`, and
`get_refresh_token()` hands over the refresh token, so they can feed
`spark_storage_conf()` like `refresh_token_from_az_cli()` does.

## Which flow

| Where Python runs | Credential | How you sign in |
| --- | --- | --- |
| anywhere, including a remote or headless machine | `DeviceCodeCredential()` | open a URL on any device, enter a code |
| your own machine, with a browser | `InteractiveBrowserCredential()` | the system browser opens; a local listener receives the code |
| a browser-hosted IDE (code-server, RStudio Server, a cloud notebook) | `InteractiveBrowserCredential(redirect_uri=...)` | open the printed URL, sign in, paste back what the callback page shows |

```python
from dazapiz import DeviceCodeCredential, spark_storage_conf

credential = DeviceCodeCredential(tenant_id="contoso.com")
conf = spark_storage_conf(refresh_token=credential)  # signs in here, once
```

The first `get_refresh_token()` (or `get_token()`) signs in. Later calls in
the same session are silent; in a later session, pass the
`AuthenticationRecord` that `credential.authenticate()` returned as
`authentication_record=` to sign in silently from the cache. On a headless
Linux machine without a usable secret store, pass
`allow_unencrypted_storage=True` to fall back to a plain file.

## Signing in from a browser-hosted session

In code-server or RStudio Server, Python runs on a server and your browser
is on your laptop. The usual browser flow starts a listener on
`localhost` of the machine running Python, which your browser never
reaches, and `azure-identity` refuses a redirect URI that is not on
localhost. `dazapiz.InteractiveBrowserCredential` does what `httr2` does in
R for such a redirect URI: it prints the sign-in URL, and you paste back
what the callback page shows.

```python
from dazapiz import InteractiveBrowserCredential

credential = InteractiveBrowserCredential(
    tenant_id="11111111-2222-3333-4444-555555555555",
    client_id="aaaaaaaa-bbbb-cccc-dddd-eeeeeeeeeeee",
    redirect_uri="https://your-domain.example/azure-callback",
)
token = credential.get_token("User.Read").token  # prompts once, then silent
```

```
Open this URL in a browser to sign in:

https://login.microsoftonline.com/11111111-.../oauth2/v2.0/authorize?client_id=...

Enter authorization code or URL:
```

After you sign in, Entra sends your browser to the redirect URI with
`?code=...&state=...`. Paste any of:

- the whole callback URL, from the address bar;
- base64-encoded JSON with `code` and `state`, as `httr2`'s callback page
  shows it;
- the bare code, and then the state when asked (`Enter state parameter:`).

MSAL checks the state and redeems the code with PKCE; a state that does not
match, an error in the callback URL, or a reply without a code raises
`ClientAuthenticationError`. The prompt needs an interactive session, a
terminal or a notebook kernel; elsewhere the credential raises
`CredentialUnavailableError` instead of waiting. No browser is opened, since
it would open on the server.

A redirect URI on `localhost` or `127.0.0.1`, or none, keeps
`azure-identity`'s own listener and browser.

## The app registration

The flow works with any Entra app registration, redirect URI and callback
page; `dazapiz` hard-codes none of them.

- **The app.** Its redirect URI must be registered under **Mobile and
  desktop applications** (a public client), because the code is redeemed
  without a client secret. A **Web** redirect needs a client secret, and an
  **SPA** one must be redeemed from the browser, so neither works.
- **The redirect URI.** Any URL your browser can load. MSAL never contacts
  it; it only has to match the registration exactly. The code-server URL
  itself works, as does a static page on any host.
- **The callback page.** It only has to let you copy the code. A page that
  shows the query string, or `httr2`'s page that shows it as base64 JSON, is
  convenient; a page that does not exist works too, since you can paste the
  URL from the address bar.

Scopes are the resource's own, such as `"User.Read"` or
`"https://storage.azure.com/.default"`. MSAL adds `offline_access`, `openid`
and `profile` itself and refuses them if you pass them. Tenant (a GUID, a
domain, `organizations` or `common`) and `authority` for sovereign clouds
are `azure-identity`'s arguments, unchanged.
